headline: High: MemMachine’s MCP/API outputs can feed xonsh’s shell and filesystem writes, creating prompt-injection, data-leakage, and cascading-action risks by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: MemMachine exposes an MCP Server and REST/Python interfaces, while xonsh can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses. That creates a plausible bridge where MemMachine output is consumed as instructions by xonsh, especially if routed through MCP or copied into shell workflows. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF MemMachine output is passed into xonsh command evaluation or shell scripts
IF an MCP tool call returns attacker-controlled text that xonsh treats as executable instructions
mitigations: Require manual review before any MemMachine output is pasted into xonsh
Disable MCP routes that return free-form instructions
Use a strict allowlist for commands accepted by xonsh
Log and diff all agent-generated shell snippets
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging from MemMachine to xonsh

B_data_leakage.rationale: MemMachine touches long-term user facts and conversational context, and xonsh reads/writes filesystem contents plus environment variables. If they share a workspace or shell session, sensitive context can be written to files or echoed into commands. The profiles do not show direct secret handling, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF MemMachine output is stored in a shared filesystem path
IF xonsh commands print or persist environment variables or notebook contents containing user facts
mitigations: Keep MemMachine and xonsh on separate workspaces
Avoid passing conversational context into shell variables
Restrict xonsh file access to a dedicated directory
Review filesystem outputs for personal data before saving
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: MemMachine has network egress and MCP/API surfaces, while xonsh has broad network egress plus shell, subprocess, and filesystem write capabilities. Even without explicit git overlap, both can mutate shared resources if pointed at the same directory or remote endpoint. The profiles do not show locking or coordination, so conflict risk is real in default multi-agent use.
conditions: IF both agents target the same filesystem directory
IF both agents act on the same remote resource or API without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize access to shared resources
Disable concurrent writes from xonsh during MemMachine runs
Use file locks for any shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level coordination primitives

D_cascading_error.rationale: MemMachine can generate context-rich outputs, and xonsh can execute shell commands and subprocesses. If xonsh treats MemMachine output as authoritative, a mistaken or malicious suggestion can become an executed action, including destructive shell operations. Because the pair lacks built-in verification in the profiles, the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF xonsh executes commands derived from MemMachine output without human verification
IF MemMachine output is used to generate scripts or notebook cells
mitigations: Require human approval before execution
Add a verification step that checks commands against policy
Run xonsh in a dry-run mode for agent-generated actions
Limit xonsh to read-only commands for agent workflows
requires-engineering: implement structured command schemas

E_compliance.rationale: MemMachine is documented as touching long-term user facts and conversational context, while xonsh handles filesystem contents and environment variables. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile, so only a low compliance concern remains from possible local handling of sensitive data. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into MemMachine and then written by xonsh to local files
IF retention or deletion policies differ between the shared workspace and agent logs
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared workflows
Set short log retention on both agents
Review local storage locations for sensitive records
Separate regulated and non-regulated tasks
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
